title: Light and Shadows
summary: Where light comes from, how it travels, which materials let it through, and how shadows form and change during the day.
poll: Shadows are more useful than most people think.

versions.title: Light and Shadows
versions.text:
Look up at the sun. It gives us light. A lamp gives light. A fire does too. The moon does not make light. It just bounces back the light of the sun.

Light moves in straight lines. It is so fast! Light from the sun gets to us in just eight minutes.

Light can pass through some things. Clear glass lets it in. We say the glass is transparent. Wood and rock let in no light. They block it. We say they are opaque. You are, too!

Stand in the sun. You block some light. A dark shape forms on the ground. That is your shadow.

Hold your hand near a lamp. Its shadow is big. Move your hand back. The shadow gets small.

At dawn, the sun is low. Your shadow is long. At noon, the sun is high. Your shadow is short.

Long ago, men used shadows to tell the time. They put a stick in the ground. They saw where its shadow fell.

In Saudi Arabia, the sun is hot. So we sit in the shade of a palm tree. Shade is a big shadow. It keeps us cool.

versions.title: Light and Shadows
versions.text:
Every morning, the sun rises and fills the world with light. Lamps and campfires also give off light. The moon shines brightly at night, but it does not make any light of its own. Instead, it bounces back light that comes from the sun.

Light always travels in straight lines, and it moves faster than anything else we know. Even though the sun is very far away, its light reaches Earth in about eight minutes.

Light can pass through some materials but not others. Clear glass lets almost all light through, so we call it transparent. Wax paper and frosted glass let only some light through. Wood, stone, and metal let no light through at all. They block the light, so we call them opaque. Your body is opaque, too.

When you stand in sunlight, your body blocks some of the light. Because light cannot bend around you, a dark area forms on the ground behind you. That dark area is your shadow.

You can change the size of a shadow. Hold your hand close to a lamp, and its shadow becomes large. Move your hand away from the lamp, and the shadow becomes smaller.

The sun changes shadows, too. In the morning, the sun is low in the sky, so shadows are long. At noon, the sun is high, so shadows are short. By evening, they stretch out again.

Long ago, people used shadows to tell the time. They placed a stick in the ground and watched where its shadow pointed.

In Saudi Arabia, summer afternoons are very hot. Many people rest in the shade of palm trees. Shade is simply a large shadow, and it keeps us cooler.

versions.title: Light and Shadows: How They Work
versions.text:
Every morning, the sun rises and fills the world with light. The sun is a light source, which means it makes its own light. Lamps, candles, and campfires are light sources, too. The moon shines brightly at night, but it is not a source. Instead, it can reflect light, bouncing back sunlight that hits its surface.

Light always travels in straight lines, and it moves faster than anything else in the universe. Even though the sun is about 150 million kilometers away, its light reaches Earth in only about eight minutes.

Different materials treat light in different ways. Clear glass and clean water let almost all light pass through, so they are transparent. Frosted glass and wax paper let some light through but scatter it, so they are translucent. Wood, stone, and metal block light completely, so they are opaque. Your body is opaque, too.

When you stand in sunlight, your body blocks some of the light. Because light cannot bend around you, a dark area forms behind you where the light cannot reach. That dark area is your shadow.

The size of a shadow depends on distance. If you hold your hand close to a lamp, it blocks more light, and the shadow becomes large. If you move your hand away, the shadow shrinks.

The position of the sun also changes shadows. In the morning and evening, the sun is low, so shadows are long. At noon, the sun is high, so shadows are short.

Long ago, people built sundials, which used the shadow of a stick to show the time of day.

In Saudi Arabia, summer afternoons are extremely hot, so people rest in the shade of palm trees. Shade is simply a large shadow that keeps us cooler.

versions.title: Light and Shadows: The Science of Darkness
versions.text:
Every morning, the rising sun fills the world with light. Scientists call the sun a light source, meaning an object that produces its own light, and electric lamps, candles, and campfires are also sources. The moon looks very bright in the night sky, but it is not a real source, because it can only reflect light, sending back the sunlight that strikes its rocky, dusty surface.

Light always travels in straight lines, and it moves faster than anything else in the universe. So, although the sun is about 150 million kilometers away, its light makes the long journey to Earth in only about eight minutes.

Different materials interact with light in different ways. Transparent materials, such as clear glass and clean water, allow almost all light to pass through them, which is why windows are made of glass. Translucent materials, such as frosted glass and wax paper, let some of the light through but scatter it in many directions, so things seen through them look blurry. Opaque materials, including wood, stone, metal, and the human body, stop light from passing through at all.

A shadow forms whenever an opaque object blocks the path of light. Because light cannot curve around objects, a dark area appears behind the object, exactly where the light cannot reach, so shadows always fall on the opposite side of an object from the light source.

The size of a shadow depends on distance. When an object is placed close to a lamp, it blocks a much wider section of the light, making a larger shadow; when the same object is moved farther away, the shadow slowly shrinks. Performers in traditional shadow puppet theaters use this idea, moving their puppets carefully to create dramatic, giant shapes.

The angle of the sun also changes shadows during the day. In the morning and evening, sunlight arrives at a low angle, so shadows stretch out long, but at midday the sun is almost directly overhead, and shadows become very short.

Centuries ago, astronomers and inventors in many civilizations, including scholars of the medieval Islamic world, designed careful sundials, which are tools that show the approximate time by following the moving shadow of a pointer. Because they depended on sunlight, however, sundials were useless at night and on cloudy days.

In Saudi Arabia, summer afternoons can be extremely hot, so families often gather in the shade of palm trees or umbrellas. Shade is simply a huge shadow, and because it blocks direct sunlight, it keeps people noticeably cooler and protects their skin.

versions.title: Light and Shadows: The Science of Darkness
versions.text:
Every morning, the rising sun floods the landscape with illumination. Scientists classify the sun as a light source, meaning an object that generates its own light energy, and electric lamps, candles, and campfires are similarly categorized as sources. The moon appears dazzlingly bright against the night sky; nevertheless, it is not a genuine source, because it can only reflect light, redirecting the sunlight that strikes its rocky, powdery surface back toward Earth.

Light always travels in straight lines, and it moves faster than anything else in the universe. Consequently, although the sun is approximately 150 million kilometers away, its light completes that extraordinary journey to Earth in approximately eight minutes.

Different materials interact with light in remarkably different ways. Transparent materials, including clear glass and clean water, allow practically all light to pass through them, which is precisely why windows are manufactured from glass. Translucent materials, such as frosted glass and waxed paper, transmit some of the light but scatter it in numerous directions, so objects viewed through them appear blurry. Opaque materials, including wood, stone, metal, and the human body, prevent light from passing through entirely.

A shadow develops whenever an opaque object interrupts the path of light. Because light cannot curve around obstacles, a darkened region appears behind the object, exactly where the light is unable to arrive, so shadows always appear on the opposite side of an object from the light source.

The size of a shadow depends substantially on distance. When an object is positioned close to a lamp, it intercepts a considerably wider section of the light, producing an enlarged shadow; when the same object is moved farther away, the shadow gradually diminishes. Performers in traditional shadow puppet theaters use this principle, positioning their figures carefully to create dramatic, enormous silhouettes.

The angle of the sun similarly transforms shadows throughout the day. During the morning and evening, sunlight arrives at a shallow angle, so shadows stretch out considerably, whereas at midday the sun is almost directly overhead, and shadows become remarkably short.

Centuries ago, astronomers and inventors in numerous civilizations, including scholars of the medieval Islamic world, designed sophisticated sundials, which are instruments that indicate the approximate time by tracking the moving shadow of a pointer. Because they depended entirely on sunlight, however, sundials were useless at night and on cloudy days.

In Saudi Arabia, summer afternoons can be intensely hot, so families frequently gather beneath the shade of palm trees or umbrellas. Shade is essentially an enormous shadow, and because it blocks direct sunlight, it keeps people noticeably cooler and protects their skin.

versions.title: Light and Shadows: The Science of Darkness
versions.text:

Scientists classify the sun as a luminous source, meaning an object that generates its own light energy, and electric lamps, candles, and campfires are similarly categorized as sources. The moon appears dazzlingly bright against the night sky; nevertheless, it is not a genuine source, because it can only reflect illumination, redirecting the sunlight that strikes its rocky, powdery surface back toward Earth.

Light invariably travels in straight lines, and it moves faster than anything else in the universe. Consequently, although the sun is positioned approximately 150 million kilometers away, its radiation completes that extraordinary journey to Earth in approximately eight minutes.

Different materials interact with light in remarkably different ways. Transparent materials, including clear glass and purified water, allow practically all illumination to pass through them, which is precisely why windows are manufactured from glass. Translucent materials, such as frosted glass and waxed paper, transmit a portion of the light but scatter it in numerous directions, so objects viewed through them appear blurry and indistinct. Opaque materials, including wood, stone, metal, and the human body, prevent illumination from penetrating entirely.

A shadow develops whenever an opaque object interrupts the path of light. Because light cannot curve around obstacles, a darkened region materializes behind the object, precisely where the illumination is unable to arrive, and shadows therefore invariably appear on the opposite side of an object from the light source.

The dimensions of a shadow depend substantially on distance. When an object is positioned close to a lamp, it intercepts a considerably wider section of the illumination, producing an enlarged shadow; when the identical object is moved farther away, the shadow gradually diminishes. Performers in traditional shadow puppet theaters exploit this principle, positioning their figures deliberately to create dramatic, enormous silhouettes.

The angle of the sun similarly transforms shadows throughout the day. During the morning and evening, sunlight arrives at a shallow angle, so shadows stretch out considerably, whereas at midday the sun is positioned almost directly overhead, and shadows become remarkably compact.

Centuries ago, astronomers and inventors in numerous civilizations, including scholars of the medieval Islamic world, designed sophisticated sundials, which are instruments that indicate the approximate time by tracking the moving shadow of a pointer. Because they depended entirely on sunlight, however, sundials were useless at night and on overcast days.

In Saudi Arabia, summer afternoons can be intensely hot, so families frequently gather beneath the shade of palm trees or umbrellas. Shade is essentially an enormous shadow, and because it obstructs direct sunlight, it keeps people noticeably cooler and protects their delicate skin.

keyWords.example: We keep the cookies in a transparent jar so we can see them.

keyWords.definition: not letting any light pass through

keyWords.definition: a cool, darker place where the sun's light is blocked

keyWords.definition: an instrument that shows the time using the shadow of a pointer
keyWords.example: The museum garden has a stone sundial that still works on sunny days.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Opaque objects block straight-moving light, making shadows that change.
The moon is the brightest light source in the night sky, brighter than any lamp.
Sundials are more accurate than modern clocks and work in all weather.
Translucent materials are the most useful choice for building windows.
questions.why: The whole article builds on how light travels and how blocking it creates shadows that change.

wrong.B: The article says the moon is not a genuine source.
wrong.C: The article says sundials were useless at night and on cloudy days.
wrong.D: The article says windows are made of transparent glass.

questions.stem: On which side of an object does its shadow always appear?
options: The side facing the light source
The opposite side from the light source
Directly underneath, at every time of day
Whichever side is coolest
questions.why: The article states that shadows always appear on the opposite side of an object from the light source.

wrong.A: The side facing the light is lit, not shaded.
wrong.C: Shadows move and stretch with the sun's angle.
wrong.D: Temperature does not decide where a shadow falls.

questions.stem: According to the article, why were sundials useless at night?
options: They were too heavy to move indoors.
Their pointers were opaque.
They depended entirely on sunlight.
The moon's light was too strong.
questions.why: The article explains that sundials depended entirely on sunlight, so they failed at night and on cloudy days.

wrong.B: An opaque pointer is what makes a sundial work.
wrong.D: The article does not say moonlight was too strong.

questions.stem: In the sentence about sunlight arriving at a shallow angle, what does angle refer to?
options: The color of the light
The speed of the light
The size of the sun
The direction from which the light comes
questions.why: The angle describes how low or high the sunlight comes in, which changes shadow length.

wrong.B: Light always travels at the same great speed.
wrong.C: The sun's size does not change during the day.

questions.stem: Why does a shadow form behind an opaque object?
options: The object makes its own darkness and spreads it.
Light cannot curve around obstacles.
The object reflects all the light back to the source.
The air behind the object is thicker and darker.
questions.why: The article says that because light cannot curve around obstacles, a dark region appears where light cannot arrive.

wrong.A: Objects do not create darkness; they block light.
wrong.C: The article does not say opaque objects send all light back.
wrong.D: The air is not mentioned as a cause.

questions.stem: A bathroom window is made of frosted glass. What is the most likely reason?
options: It blocks all light so the room stays dark.
It makes the room hotter.
It lets light in while making shapes blurry, which gives privacy.
It reflects all sunlight away from the house.
questions.why: Frosted glass is translucent, so it lets in some light but makes things seen through it look blurry.

wrong.A: Frosted glass lets some light through, so it does not block all light.
wrong.B: The article does not connect frosted glass with heat.
wrong.D: Translucent glass transmits light rather than reflecting all of it.

questions.stem: A performer moves a puppet away from the lamp during a show. What will the audience most likely see?
options: The puppet's shadow gets smaller.
The shadow grows enormous.
The shadow moves to the same side as the lamp.
The shadow disappears completely.
questions.why: The article explains that moving an object farther from a lamp makes its shadow diminish.

wrong.B: The shadow grows when the puppet moves closer, not farther.
wrong.C: Shadows fall on the opposite side from the light.
wrong.D: The puppet still blocks light, so a smaller shadow remains.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with shade in Saudi Arabia?
options: To argue that palm trees are better than umbrellas
To explain how sundials were invented
To prove that the moon is not a light source
To connect the science of shadows to readers' everyday lives
questions.why: Shade is a familiar shadow in hot Saudi afternoons, so the ending links the science to daily life.

wrong.A: The article mentions both and does not compare them.
wrong.B: Sundials are discussed in an earlier paragraph.
wrong.C: The moon is discussed at the beginning.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say shadows are just darkness and are not useful. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with at least two examples from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two examples from the article.
I explained how each example supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that shadows are just darkness with no use, because the article gives two clear examples of how people use them. First, ancient people built sundials, which used the shadow of a stick at a certain angle to tell the time of day. Second, people in hot places like Saudi Arabia rest in the shade of palm trees, which is really just a large, cool shadow that blocks the opaque leaves' sunlight. Both examples show that shadows can be genuinely useful, not just dark empty space.
